title: Liquid I.V. vs Gatorade: Which Is Better for a Hangover?
excerpt: Liquid I.V. vs Gatorade compared on sodium, potassium, sugar, and cost, plus Gatorade Zero and Gatorlyte, and which to grab the morning after drinking.
metaDescription: Liquid I.V. vs Gatorade for a hangover: sodium, potassium, sugar, and cost compared, plus Gatorade Zero and Gatorlyte, and which one to grab.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for the morning after drinking, Liquid I.V. is the better rehydration drink. One stick has roughly twice the sodium of a 20-ounce bottle of regular Gatorade, about five times the potassium, and about a third of the sugar. That recipe is much closer to the medical rehydration drinks doctors use for stomach bugs. Gatorade isn't useless, though. It's cheaper per serving in some places, it's already mixed, it's in every gas station, and for a mild hangover the gap between the two is small. Neither one fixes the parts of a hangover that come from alcohol itself, like nausea, fatigue, and brain fog.

**The quick rules:** If you're properly dried out (a long night, a hot room, some vomiting), pick Liquid I.V. or a similar high-sodium mix, or Gatorade's own **Gatorlyte**, which is the closest thing in the Gatorade lineup. If it's a mild hangover and Gatorade is what's in the fridge, drink it slowly and eat something salty with it. If you're watching sugar, **Gatorade Zero** or **Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free** both keep the electrolytes. And don't drink three of either one, because the sodium or the sugar adds up fast.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article compares consumer products and explains general research in plain words. It is not medical advice. **Get medical help if** you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, you've vomited repeatedly, you see blood in vomit or stool, or you have signs of serious dehydration: dizziness or fainting when you stand, confusion, a racing heart that won't settle, very dark urine, or little or no urine for many hours. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room** if someone who has been drinking is very hard to wake, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no electrolyte drink helps. **Talk to your doctor before using electrolyte mixes regularly** if you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, or you take medicines that change your sodium or potassium levels, such as some blood pressure pills and water pills.

## Liquid I.V. vs Gatorade: The Numbers Side by Side

The difference between these two drinks is mostly about two things: how much salt they carry and how much sugar comes with it. Here are approximate label figures for the most common versions. Formulas and serving sizes change, so check the package you're actually holding.

| Per serving (approx.) | Serving | Sodium | Potassium | Sugar | Calories |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Liquid I.V. Hydration Multiplier (original) | 1 stick in 16 fl oz water | ~500 mg | ~370 mg | ~11 g | ~45 |
| Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free | 1 stick in 16 fl oz water | ~500 mg | ~370 mg | 0 g | ~15 or less |
| Gatorade Thirst Quencher (regular) | 20 fl oz bottle | ~270 mg | ~75 mg | ~34 g | ~140 |
| Gatorade Zero | 20 fl oz bottle | ~270 mg | ~75 mg | 0 g | ~10 |
| G2 (lower sugar) | 20 fl oz bottle | ~270 mg | ~75 mg | ~12 g | ~50 |
| Gatorlyte | 20 fl oz bottle | ~490 mg | ~350 mg | ~12 g | ~50 |

A few things jump out:

- **Liquid I.V. carries almost twice the sodium in less liquid.** A stick goes into 16 ounces of water, while a Gatorade bottle is 20 ounces. So the drink you actually swallow is roughly two and a half times saltier per sip. That's on purpose.
- **Regular Gatorade has about three times the sugar.** Around 34 grams is close to what's in a 12-ounce can of soda. Liquid I.V. has about 11 grams.
- **Potassium isn't close.** Liquid I.V. has several hundred milligrams; classic Gatorade has well under a hundred.
- **Gatorade Zero removes the sugar but not the gap.** It has the same modest sodium and potassium as the regular version.
- **Gatorlyte is the Gatorade that competes.** Its sodium, potassium, and sugar land very close to a stick of Liquid I.V.

Liquid I.V. also adds several vitamins, including vitamin C and some B vitamins. Those look good on the box, but they do very little for a hangover. You aren't short on vitamin C because you had five beers, and there's no good evidence that extra B vitamins ease next-day symptoms in people who eat normally.

## Why the Salt-to-Sugar Ratio Matters

This is the part that explains the whole comparison, and it's simpler than the marketing makes it sound.

Your small intestine has a built-in way of pulling water into your body. It absorbs **sodium and glucose together**, using the same carrier in the gut wall, and water follows them across. Doctors figured this out decades ago while trying to treat cholera and other diarrheal diseases. The result was **oral rehydration solution (ORS)**: a drink with a lot of salt, a modest amount of sugar, and water. It's one of the most important medical advances of the last century, because it lets people recover from serious fluid loss without an IV.

The World Health Organization's current ORS recipe works out to roughly 1,700 mg of sodium and about 13.5 grams of glucose per liter. Here's roughly where our two drinks sit when you scale them to a liter:

| Per liter (approx.) | Sodium | Sugar |
|---|---|---|
| WHO oral rehydration solution | ~1,700 mg | ~13.5 g glucose |
| Liquid I.V. (original, mixed as directed) | ~1,050 mg | ~23 g |
| Regular Gatorade | ~460 mg | ~58 g |

So Liquid I.V. sits between a medical rehydration drink and a sports drink, closer to the medical end on sodium. Regular Gatorade has about a quarter of the sodium concentration of ORS and roughly four times the sugar.

Liquid I.V. calls its approach "Cellular Transport Technology." Take away the brand name and it's the sodium-and-glucose principle above. That doesn't make it a gimmick. It means the science is real, decades old, and not owned by anybody. Any drink with a similar salt-to-sugar balance does the same job.

Gatorade comes from a different starting point. It was developed in the 1960s at the University of Florida for football players sweating hard in the heat. Athletes in the middle of a workout burn through carbohydrate, so the formula leans on sugar for fuel and flavor, with a lighter dose of salt. That's a sensible design for a long practice. It's not the ideal design for someone lying on a couch who is short on fluid and hasn't burned any energy since midnight.

### Does extra sugar hurt?

A little sugar helps your gut absorb sodium and water. A lot of sugar doesn't add much more benefit. A very sweet drink can also sit badly on a queasy stomach, and a sugar-heavy drink pulls a bit of water into the gut before it's absorbed. For most people with an ordinary hangover, this is a small effect. It matters more if you're nauseous or if you're drinking several bottles to try to feel better.

## What These Drinks Can and Can't Fix in a Hangover

It helps to be clear about what a hangover actually is, because electrolyte drinks only reach one piece of it.

Alcohol lowers **vasopressin**, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water. With less of it around, your kidneys let more water through, and some sodium and potassium go with it. Add a warm bar, dancing, hours of sleep without a sip of water, and maybe some vomiting, and it's easy to wake up short on fluid.

Dehydration explains some symptoms well:

- Dry mouth and strong thirst
- Part of the headache
- Feeling lightheaded when you stand up
- Dark yellow urine

But many hangover symptoms come from other causes, and no drink, however well balanced, touches them:

- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, before breaking it down further. It's linked to nausea, flushing, and the general poisoned feeling.
- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response, a bit like being mildly sick. That's a big part of why you feel achy, foggy, and flat.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol can help you fall asleep but breaks up the second half of the night, so you wake up tired no matter how much fluid you drink.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and raises acid, which adds to nausea and heartburn.
- **Low blood sugar, for some people.** Alcohol can interfere with how your liver releases sugar, which adds to shakiness and weakness. This is the one place the sugar in regular Gatorade or Liquid I.V. can actually help.

Researchers who study hangovers have also found that how dehydrated someone is doesn't line up neatly with how bad their hangover feels. Rehydrating helps, but it isn't a cure. That's why both of these drinks are best thought of as "fix the thirst and the dry-mouth headache" tools, not hangover cures. Our guide to [whether water helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover) goes deeper into what fluid alone can and can't do.

## Liquid I.V. for a Hangover: Pros and Cons

**What it does well**

- Strong sodium dose per serving, which is the electrolyte that matters most for holding onto fluid
- Real potassium, which you also lose when you urinate more
- Moderate sugar that helps absorption without turning it into soda
- Portable sticks you can keep in a bag, a desk drawer, or a hotel room
- Sugar-free version for people limiting sugar or carbs

**Where it falls short**

- It costs more per serving than store-brand rehydration powders with similar labels
- Some people find the taste very salty or very sweet, especially when they're queasy
- At around 500 mg of sodium per stick, a few sticks plus a salty breakfast adds up quickly
- The added vitamins are mostly marketing for this purpose
- You need water and a glass or bottle, which is one more step when you feel awful

We cover timing, dose, and the Energy and Sleep versions in detail in our [Liquid I.V. for a hangover](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover) guide. Short version on those: the Energy line adds caffeine, which can help a foggy morning but may worsen jitters or a racing heart, and the Sleep line adds melatonin and other ingredients that you shouldn't combine with alcohol the same night.

## Gatorade for a Hangover: Pros and Cons

**What it does well**

- Already mixed and cold, ready to drink
- Sold almost everywhere, at any hour
- The sugar can help the shaky, low-energy feeling, especially if you haven't eaten
- Many people find it easy to drink when plain water seems unappealing
- Gatorade Zero and G2 give lower-sugar options, and Gatorlyte gives a high-electrolyte option

**Where it falls short**

- Regular Gatorade is light on sodium and very light on potassium for real rehydration
- About 34 grams of sugar per 20-ounce bottle, which adds up if you drink two or three
- A sweet drink can make nausea worse for some people
- Plastic bottles are bulky to stock compared with powder sticks

Our [Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/gatorade-for-hangover) page walks through each version in more detail, including whether flavor matters (it doesn't).

## Liquid I.V. vs Gatorade Zero

This is a common matchup for people avoiding sugar. Gatorade Zero keeps the same electrolytes as regular Gatorade and replaces the sugar with no-calorie sweeteners. So it's lighter on sodium and potassium than any version of Liquid I.V.

If you want sugar-free and you want the stronger rehydration drink, **Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free** is the better match. It keeps roughly the same sodium and potassium as the original and swaps the sugar for sweeteners such as allulose. The trade-off with any sugar-free mix is that you lose the small glucose boost that helps absorption. If you're eating breakfast alongside it, the food makes up for that.

One note for sensitive stomachs: some sweeteners, including sugar alcohols and allulose, can cause bloating or loose stools in larger amounts. After a night of drinking, when your gut may already be unsettled, start with one serving and see how it sits.

## Liquid I.V. vs Gatorlyte

If you like Gatorade but want something that actually behaves like a rehydration drink, Gatorlyte is the answer. Per 20-ounce bottle it has around 490 mg of sodium, about 350 mg of potassium, and around 12 grams of sugar. That's nearly the same as a stick of Liquid I.V., delivered in a little more liquid.

In practice the choice comes down to convenience and price:

- **Gatorlyte** is ready to drink and easy to grab from a store on the way home. It usually costs more than regular Gatorade.
- **Liquid I.V.** sticks are easier to keep on hand and take nowhere near as much space.

For rehydration, treat them as roughly equal. Pick whichever you'll actually have when you need it.

## Which Is Healthier: Liquid I.V. or Gatorade?

"Healthier" depends on what you're comparing and why you're drinking it.

- **For rehydration after drinking or being sick:** Liquid I.V. (or Gatorlyte) wins, because it has the salt-to-sugar balance that rehydrates you more efficiently.
- **For sugar intake:** Liquid I.V. original has about a third of the sugar of a bottle of regular Gatorade. The sugar-free versions of both have none.
- **For sodium intake:** Gatorade is lower. If you've been told to limit salt, regular Gatorade or Gatorade Zero puts less sodium in your day than Liquid I.V. does. US dietary guidelines suggest most adults keep total sodium under about 2,300 mg a day, and one stick of Liquid I.V. is around a fifth of that.
- **For everyday drinking when you aren't dehydrated:** neither one is necessary. Water is fine. Electrolyte drinks are tools for when you've actually lost fluid, not something healthy adults need with every meal.

So neither drink is "healthy" or "unhealthy" on its own. Liquid I.V. is the better tool for real dehydration, and Gatorade is the gentler choice on salt but heavier on sugar.

## Cost: Which Is the Better Value?

Prices change a lot by store, pack size, and sales, so treat these as rough ranges rather than quotes. A single stick of Liquid I.V. bought in a multipack usually works out to somewhere around one to two dollars. A 20-ounce bottle of Gatorade often costs one to three dollars depending on whether you buy it singly at a gas station or in a case at a grocery store. Gatorlyte typically costs more per bottle than classic Gatorade.

The fairer way to judge value is cost per useful dose of electrolytes. To get the sodium in one stick of Liquid I.V., you'd need almost two bottles of regular Gatorade, along with nearly 70 grams of sugar. On that measure, Liquid I.V. is the better value for rehydration. If you want the same recipe for less, store-brand oral rehydration powders and Pedialyte often match Liquid I.V.'s label at a lower price. The trick is to compare the nutrition panel, not the brand: if a cheaper powder lands within about 100 mg of Liquid I.V. on sodium and has similar potassium and sugar, it will do the same job.

## Which One Should You Grab? A Simple Guide by Situation

**Mild hangover, you had dinner, you just feel a bit dry.** Either is fine. Honestly, water and a normal breakfast probably cover you. If Gatorade is what you have, drink one bottle slowly.

**Long night, little food, woke up very thirsty with a pounding head.** Liquid I.V. or Gatorlyte. The higher sodium makes a real difference when you're actually short on fluid.

**You threw up last night or this morning.** Pick the higher-sodium, lower-sugar option, and take small sips every few minutes rather than gulping. If you can't keep anything down for many hours, stop trying at home and get medical help.

**You were sweating too.** A summer wedding, a festival, a hot bar, a night of dancing. Alcohol and sweat together drain more sodium. Go with Liquid I.V. or Gatorlyte.

**You're watching sugar or you have diabetes.** Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free if you want the stronger electrolytes, Gatorade Zero if you want less sodium. If you have diabetes, alcohol can also cause low blood sugar many hours later, so talk to your doctor about how to handle a night out.

**You're on a salt-restricted diet.** Talk to your doctor before using a high-sodium mix. Regular water plus normal food may be all you need.

**You can't face anything sweet.** Try Liquid I.V. mixed with a bit more water than directed, or skip both and have water with salty crackers or broth.

## How to Drink It for the Best Results

A few habits make either drink work better:

1. **Sip, don't chug.** Drinking a whole bottle fast on an upset stomach is a good way to bring it back up. Spread one serving over 20 to 30 minutes.
2. **Eat something.** Toast, eggs, a banana, soup, or salty crackers. Food helps your blood sugar, settles your stomach, and adds more sodium and potassium. If eggs sound good, our [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) piece explains why they're a solid pick.
3. **Stick to one or two servings.** More doesn't mean faster recovery. After one or two, switch to plain water.
4. **Check your urine.** Pale yellow means you're doing fine. Very dark urine or very little of it after several hours of drinking fluids is a sign to take dehydration more seriously.
5. **Consider a serving before bed.** A glass of an electrolyte drink and some water before sleep can mean you wake up less dried out. Our guide on [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers timing in more detail.

### A warning about plain water on an empty stomach

Plain water is fine for most hangovers. The one situation to avoid is drinking several liters of plain water very quickly while eating nothing, especially after vomiting. Water without salt replaces fluid but not sodium, and in extreme cases that can dilute the sodium in your blood. It's rare and takes real effort, but it's the reason an electrolyte drink or some salty food is a good idea when you've lost a lot of fluid.

## What About Pedialyte, Coconut Water, and Other Options?

Liquid I.V. and Gatorade aren't the only choices:

- **Pedialyte** was designed as a medical rehydration drink. It has much more sodium and potassium than regular Gatorade, with less sugar, and sits in a similar range to Liquid I.V. We compare it head to head in our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade hangover guide](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover).
- **Coconut water** is high in potassium but fairly low in sodium. It's gentle and pleasant, but it's not a full replacement for an electrolyte drink. More in our [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) guide.
- **Broth or soup** is an underrated option: salty, warm, easy on the stomach, and it counts as food.
- **Pharmacy oral rehydration salts** follow the WHO-style recipe closely and are usually the cheapest strong option.

For a broader ranked list, see our [electrolyte drinks for hangovers compared](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) guide. Related head-to-heads: [Drip Drop vs Liquid I.V.](/never-hungover/drip-drop-vs-liquid-iv), [LMNT vs Liquid I.V.](/never-hungover/lmnt-vs-liquid-iv), and [Electrolit vs Pedialyte](/never-hungover/electrolit-vs-pedialyte). On a budget, try our [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink).

## Who Should Be Careful With Either Drink

Both drinks are safe for most healthy adults in normal amounts. Be more careful, and check with a doctor or pharmacist before regular use, if you:

- Have **high blood pressure** or have been told to limit salt
- Have **kidney disease**, where extra potassium and sodium can be hard to clear
- Have **heart failure** or another condition where fluid and salt intake are managed closely
- Have **diabetes** and need to count sugar (or you're using alcohol and insulin or other blood-sugar medicines together)
- Take medicines that **raise potassium**, such as some blood pressure drugs (ACE inhibitors and ARBs) or potassium-sparing water pills

Also remember these drinks aren't a reason to drink more. They make the morning a little easier. They don't change how much alcohol your body has to process.

## Getting Ahead of the Hangover Instead

Rehydration is a cleanup job. The steps with the best evidence for a better morning happen the night before: eat a real meal before you drink, pace yourself to roughly one drink an hour, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and stop earlier than you think you need to. Our guide to [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through each habit.

Some people also take **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, before or while drinking. Research, mostly in animals and lab studies with limited human data, suggests it may affect how the body handles alcohol and acetaldehyde, the part of a hangover that no electrolyte drink can reach. It's promising, not proven. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers outright, and it doesn't replace drinking less, eating, or staying hydrated. If you want to try it, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- **Liquid I.V. is the stronger rehydration drink.** About twice the sodium of a 20-ounce Gatorade, several times the potassium, and about a third of the sugar.
- **Regular Gatorade still helps** with a mild hangover, especially paired with food, but it's mostly sugar water with a modest pinch of salt.
- **Gatorlyte closes the gap.** If you prefer Gatorade, it's the version that matches Liquid I.V. on electrolytes.
- **For sugar-free, Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free beats Gatorade Zero** on electrolytes, while Gatorade Zero is lower in sodium.
- **Neither fixes the whole hangover.** They help thirst, dry mouth, and part of the headache. Nausea, fatigue, and brain fog come mostly from alcohol's other effects.
- **Get medical help** if you can't keep fluids down, have signs of serious dehydration, or see any signs of alcohol poisoning.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Liquid I.V. better than Gatorade for a hangover?**

For rehydration, yes. A stick of Liquid I.V. has roughly 500 mg of sodium, 370 mg of potassium, and 11 grams of sugar, compared with about 270 mg of sodium, 75 mg of potassium, and 34 grams of sugar in a 20-ounce bottle of regular Gatorade. That balance is closer to a medical rehydration drink. For a mild hangover where you've eaten, the difference is small, and neither one fixes the nausea or fatigue that come from alcohol itself.

**Is Liquid I.V. better than Gatorade Zero?**

For electrolytes, yes. Gatorade Zero removes the sugar but keeps the same modest sodium and potassium as regular Gatorade, so it's a lighter rehydration drink than either version of Liquid I.V. If you want sugar-free with stronger electrolytes, Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free is the closer fit. If you're trying to keep sodium low, Gatorade Zero puts less salt in your day.

**Which is healthier, Liquid I.V. or Gatorade?**

It depends on the goal. Liquid I.V. has much less sugar than regular Gatorade and more electrolytes, which makes it the better tool when you're actually dehydrated. Gatorade has less sodium, which matters if you've been told to limit salt. For everyday drinking when you aren't dehydrated, neither is necessary and plain water is fine.

**Is Gatorlyte the same as Liquid I.V.?**

They're different products, but their labels are very close. Gatorlyte has around 490 mg of sodium, 350 mg of potassium, and 12 grams of sugar per 20-ounce bottle, which is nearly the same as a stick of Liquid I.V. For hangover rehydration, treat them as roughly equal and choose based on price and convenience.

**How many Liquid I.V. sticks or Gatorades should I drink for a hangover?**

One or two servings is usually enough, then switch to plain water and eat something. Each Liquid I.V. stick has around 500 mg of sodium, so three sticks plus a salty breakfast can push you past a day's recommended sodium. Three bottles of regular Gatorade is over 100 grams of sugar. If you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, talk to your doctor before using either regularly.

**Should I drink Liquid I.V. or Gatorade before bed after drinking?**

A serving of an electrolyte drink plus some water before sleep can help you wake up less dried out, and many people find that easier than dealing with thirst in the morning. Choose the lower-sugar options if you're watching sugar. It won't prevent a hangover by itself, because dehydration is only one part of what causes one.

**Can Liquid I.V. or Gatorade cure a hangover?**

No. Both can ease the symptoms that come from dehydration, like thirst, dry mouth, and part of the headache. Much of a hangover comes from acetaldehyde, inflammation, poor sleep, and stomach irritation, and electrolyte drinks don't address those. Time, food, rest, and fluids are still the core of recovery.

**When should I see a doctor instead of drinking electrolytes?**

Get medical help if you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, keep vomiting, see blood in vomit or stool, or have signs of serious dehydration such as fainting, confusion, a racing heart, or very little urine. Call 911 if someone who has been drinking is hard to wake, breathing slowly, having a seizure, or has cold or bluish skin, because those are signs of alcohol poisoning.
